title: Information
body:
$$
I(x) = -\log_2 P(x) = \log_2 \frac{1}{P(x)}
$$

**Surprise, measured in bits.** How much you learn from being told that $x$ happened. A certain
event ($P = 1$) carries $I = 0$: you already knew, so hearing it teaches you nothing. A
one-in-a-million event carries about 20 bits. As $P \to 0$, $I \to \infty$.

Note this is a property of the *outcome*, not of the distribution. [[Shannon Entropy]] is the
average of it over all outcomes, and that is the difference between the two notes.

## Why the logarithm, specifically

Not an arbitrary choice. Three requirements pin it down almost uniquely:

1. **Monotone decreasing in $P$.** Rarer things are more informative.
2. **Zero at $P = 1$.** A certainty tells you nothing.
3. **Additive over independent events.** Learning two unrelated facts should give you the sum of
   what each gives you separately.

Requirement 3 is the one that forces the log. Independent events multiply their probabilities
($P(x,y) = P(x)P(y)$) while information must add, and the log is the function that turns products
into sums. Nothing else does.

## Bits

Base 2 makes the unit the bit, and it is literal rather than metaphorical: a fair coin flip has
$P = \tfrac12$ so $I = 1$ bit, and $n$ fair flips carry $n$ bits. That is exactly the
[[Integer Representation]] statement that $n$ bits distinguish $2^n$ equally likely things, read in
the other direction. Base $e$ gives nats and base 10 gives dits; only the constant changes, so
which base you use never affects an argument.

The practical reading is **code length**. An outcome of probability $P$ deserves a codeword of
about $-\log_2 P$ bits, spending short codes on common outcomes and long ones on rare, which is why
[[Shannon Entropy]] turns out to be the average length of the best possible code.

- [[Cross-Entropy]], [[KL Divergence]]: what happens when you use the wrong probabilities

  comes from and what $\mathbf{E}[\cdot]$ means
